propositions.text: A drug patent holder can protect its patent from infringement under the Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations.
propositions.quote: A company that holds a drug patent can protect the patent from infringement by other companies under rules set out in patented medicine regulations: Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations, SOR/93-133 [Regulations]

propositions.text: Patent protection begins when the Minister of Health lists the patent on the register.
propositions.quote: That protection begins when the Minister of Health lists the patent on the patent register.

propositions.text: The listing date is critical.
propositions.quote: The listing date is critical.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that patent protection under the Regulations starts when the Minister lists the patent, making the listing date crucial.

propositions.text: Serono argues the Minister unreasonably delayed listing their patent, causing loss of patent rights.
propositions.quote: The applicants [collectively, Serono] are drug companies who argue that the Minister unreasonably delayed listing their patent on the register, resulting in a loss of their patent rights.

propositions.text: Serono claims the Minister's approach fails to respect statutory, regulatory, treaty obligations, and the Minister’s own policies.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s approach to listing patents, says Serono, fails to respect statutory, regulatory, and treaty obligations, as well as the Minister’s own policies.

propositions.text: Serono asks to quash the Minister’s decision and declare the patent listed as of the earlier, proper date.
propositions.quote: Serono asks me to quash the Minister’s decision and declare the patent listed as of the earlier date on which the Minister should have added it to the register.

propositions.text: Intervener Innovative Medicines Canada supports Serono’s position.
propositions.quote: The intervener Innovative Medicines Canada [IMC] supports Serono’s position.

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues the Minister delayed listing their patent, violating obligations, and seeks to quash the decision; IMC supports Serono.

propositions.text: The Minister of Health and Apotex argue the Minister’s approach was reasonable and legally sound.
propositions.quote: the Minister of Health and Apotex, supported by the intervener the Canadian Generic Pharmaceutical Association [CGPA] – argue that the Minister’s approach was reasonable and legally sound.

propositions.text: Respondents ask to dismiss Serono’s application for judicial review.
propositions.quote: The respondents ask me to dismiss Serono’s application for judicial review of the Minister’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister, Apotex, and CGPA argue the Minister acted reasonably and seek dismissal of Serono’s judicial review application.

propositions.text: The sole issue is whether the Minister’s decision was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The sole issue is whether the Minister’s decision was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the only issue as whether the Minister’s decision was unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Minister’s decision on the listing date was not unreasonable under the Regulations and case law.
propositions.quote: I find that the Minister’s decision on the listing date for Serono’s patent was not unreasonable in light of the governing Regulations and case law.

propositions.text: The Minister adds patents to the register when they are eligible for listing – not sooner, not later.
propositions.quote: The Minister adds patents to the register when they are eligible for listing – not sooner, not later.

propositions.text: The court must dismiss Serono’s application for judicial review.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, I must dismiss Serono’s application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Minister’s decision reasonable, as patents are listed when eligible, and dismisses Serono’s application.

propositions.text: The Regulations call drug patent holders 'first persons' and generic drug companies 'second persons.'
propositions.quote: The Regulations refer to drug patent holders as “first persons” and generic drug companies as “second persons.”

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Regulations' terminology for patent holders and generic companies.

propositions.text: The Minister must maintain a register of patents for approved drugs and decide if a patent meets eligibility requirements before listing.
propositions.quote: The Regulations impose on the Minister an obligation to maintain a register of patents for approved drugs. Before listing a patent, the Minister must decide whether the patent meets the requirements of the Regulations

propositions.text: Eligibility requires the patent to relate to an approved medicine, formulation, dosage form, or use (s 4(2)).
propositions.quote: whether the patent relates to an approved medicine, contains a claim for an approved formulation of that medicine, identifies a claim for an approved dosage form, or specifies an approved use of the medicine (s 4(2)).

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines the Minister’s duty to maintain the register and the eligibility requirements for listing a patent.

propositions.text: Once a patent is listed, second persons are prohibited from entering the market for the same medicine except under strict conditions (s 7(1)).
propositions.quote: Once the Minister has added a patent to the register, the Regulations prohibit second persons from entering the market for the same medicine, except in accordance with strict conditions (s 7(1)).

propositions.text: A second person seeking to market a generic must address any patents already listed (ss 5(1) and 5(4)).
propositions.quote: a second person who seeks to market a generic version of the patented drug must first address any patents already listed on the register (ss 5(1) and 5(4)).

propositions.text: This arrangement is called the 'frozen register' because it freezes in time the patents a second person must address.
propositions.quote: This regulatory arrangement is often referred to as the “frozen register” because it freezes in time the patents that a second person must address.

propositions.text: Second persons can address listed patents by agreeing not to enter until expiry, obtaining consent, or alleging invalidity/non-infringement (s 5(2.1)).
propositions.quote: The second person can address the listed patents by accepting that it will not enter the market until the patents expire, by obtaining the first person’s consent, or by alleging that the patent is invalid or would not be infringed by the second person’s product (s 5(2.1)).

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the 'frozen register' system and how second persons must address listed patents before entering the market.

propositions.text: If a second person alleges invalidity or non-infringement, it must serve a Notice of Allegation (NOA) on the first person (s 5(3)).
propositions.quote: Where the second person asserts that the listed patent is invalid or would not be infringed, it must serve a Notice of Allegation [NOA] on the first person (s 5(3)).

propositions.text: The first person can bring an action for a declaration of infringement (s 6(1)).
propositions.quote: The first person can then bring an action for a declaration that the second person’s product would infringe the patent (s 6(1)).

propositions.text: Such an action bars the Minister from allowing the second person to enter the market for 24 months (s 7(1)(d)).
propositions.quote: The action bars the Minister from allowing the second person to enter the market for 24 months (s 7(1)(d)).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the NOA process and the resulting 24-month bar on market entry for second persons.

propositions.text: Serono filed its application for the '419 patent in December 2005, titled 'Cladribine Regimen for Treating Multiple Sclerosis.'
propositions.quote: Serono filed its application for Canadian Patent No 3,087,419 [the ‘419 patent] in December 2005. The patent is entitled “Cladribine Regimen for Treating Multiple Sclerosis.”

propositions.text: CIPO granted the '419 patent on March 7, 2023.
propositions.quote: The Canadian Intellectual Property Office [CIPO] granted the ‘419 patent on March 7, 2023.

paragraphs.summary: Serono applied for the '419 patent in 2005, and CIPO granted it on March 7, 2023.

propositions.text: On March 16, 2023, Serono submitted patent lists for the '419 patent against MAVENCLAD.
propositions.quote: On March 16, 2023, 9 days after the granting of the patent, Serono submitted patent lists for the ‘419 patent against a product called MAVENCLAD

propositions.text: Health Canada screened the lists the next day and did a preliminary eligibility analysis on March 21, 2023.
propositions.quote: Health Canada screened the patent lists the next day and then, on March 21, 2023, carried out a preliminary analysis of the patent’s eligibility for listing.

propositions.text: On March 23, 2023, OSIP informed Serono the lists were added to the register as of that date.
propositions.quote: On March 23, 2023, the Office of Submissions and Intellectual Property [OSIP] informed Serono by letter that its patent lists had been added to the register as of that date – March 23, 2023

propositions.text: The addition was one week after Serono submitted its patent lists.
propositions.quote: March 23, 2023, one week after Serono submitted its patent lists for the ‘419 patent.

paragraphs.summary: Serono submitted patent lists on March 16, 2023; OSIP added them to the register on March 23, 2023, after screening and analysis.

propositions.text: On March 22, 2023, Apotex filed a regulatory submission for a generic MAVENCLAD.
propositions.quote: One day earlier, on March 22, 2023, Apotex filed its regulatory submission for a generic version of MAVENCLAD.

propositions.text: Because Serono’s patent lists were not yet on the register, Apotex did not have to address the '419 patent.
propositions.quote: Because Serono’s patent lists had not yet been added to the register, it appeared that Apotex did not have to address the ‘419 patent.

paragraphs.summary: Apotex filed for a generic MAVENCLAD on March 22, 2023, before Serono’s patent was listed, so it did not have to address the patent.

propositions.text: On April 20, 2023, Serono asked OSIP to reconsider the listing date, arguing it should be March 16, 2023.
propositions.quote: on April 20, 2023, Serono asked OSIP to reconsider the listing date of March 23, 2023, arguing that the proper date should have been the date on which it had submitted its patent lists – March 16, 2023.

propositions.text: If the date were March 16, Apotex would have had to address the '419 patent on March 22, 2023.
propositions.quote: Based on that date, Apotex would have had to address the ‘419 patent on March 22, 2023.

paragraphs.summary: Serono requested OSIP to change the listing date to March 16, which would have required Apotex to address the patent.

propositions.text: OSIP informed Serono that the Minister maintained the listing date of March 23, 2023, the eligibility decision date.
propositions.quote: OSIP informed Serono that the Minister maintained the listing date of March 23, 2023, the date of the eligibility decision.

paragraphs.summary: OSIP told Serono the Minister would keep the listing date as March 23, 2023, the eligibility decision date.

propositions.text: The Minister noted the Regulations distinguish between submitting a patent list and adding a patent to the register.
propositions.quote: The Minister observed that the Regulations distinguish between submitting a patent list and adding a patent to the register.

propositions.text: The Minister must add only patents that meet eligibility requirements and refuse those that do not (s 3(2)).
propositions.quote: The Minister must maintain a register of patents that have been submitted for listing by adding those patents that meet the applicable eligibility requirements, and by refusing to add patents that do not meet those requirements (s 3(2)).

propositions.text: A patent is eligible if it claims an approved medicinal ingredient, formulation, dosage form, or use (s 4(2)).
propositions.quote: A patent is eligible to be added to the register if it claims an approved medicinal ingredient, formulation, dosage form, or use (s 4(2)).

paragraphs.summary: The Minister found the Regulations distinguish between submitting and adding patents, and only eligible patents are added to the register.

propositions.text: The Minister cited s 5(1) and s 5(2.1) to reinforce the distinction between submission and addition to the register.
propositions.quote: The Minister also cited the distinction between submission of a patent list and the addition of patents to the register in s 5(1) of the Regulations.

propositions.text: Second persons must address submitted patent lists, but NOA statements must target patents included on the register (s 5(2.1)).
propositions.quote: However, the statements and allegations in the second person’s NOA must be directed at patents that are included on the register (s 5(2.1)).

propositions.text: These provisions reinforce the distinction between submission and addition to the register.
propositions.quote: these provisions reinforce the distinction between the submission of patent lists and the addition of patents to the register.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister found that the Regulations reinforce the distinction between submitting a patent list and adding a patent to the register.

propositions.text: The Minister rejected Serono’s argument that eligible patent lists should be added to the register on the submission date.
propositions.quote: The Minister rejected Serono’s argument that eligible patent lists should be added to the register on the date they are submitted

propositions.text: The Minister pointed out that second persons do not have to address patents added on or after the date of their submission for a notice of compliance (ss 5(1),(4)).
propositions.quote: The Minister pointed out that the Regulations provide that second persons do not have to address patents that were added to the register on or after the date the second person filed its submission for a notice of compliance (ss 5(1),(4)).

propositions.text: The regulatory provisions confirm the distinction between submission and addition to the register.
propositions.quote: Again, the regulatory provisions confirm the distinction between the submission of patent lists and the addition of patents to the register.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister rejected Serono’s argument and found the Regulations confirm the distinction between submission and addition dates.

propositions.text: The Minister cited the 2006 RIAS as confirming that second persons must address patents eligible for and actually added to the register.
propositions.quote: the RIAS confirms that the Regulations require second persons to address patents that are eligible for addition to the register, and that have actually been added to the register.

propositions.text: The Minister cited Health Canada’s Guidance Document, which supports using the eligibility decision date, not the submission date, for listing.
propositions.quote: the correct date for adding a patent to the register is the date on which it was found to be eligible, not the date on which it was submitted

paragraphs.summary: The Minister relied on the 2006 RIAS and Health Canada’s Guidance Document to support using the eligibility decision date for listing.

propositions.text: The Minister found the Regulations aim to balance patent enforcement with timely generic entry.
propositions.quote: the purpose of the Regulations is to “balance effective patent enforcement over new and innovative drugs with the timely entry of their lower priced generic competitors.”

propositions.text: That balance would be upset if second persons had to address patents added after their submissions.
propositions.quote: that balance would be upset if second persons had to address patents added to the register after they had already filed their submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister found the Regulations balance patent rights and generic entry, which would be upset by retroactive listing dates.

propositions.text: The Minister found support in Eli Lilly 2009 FC 474, where the court held second persons must address patents added to the register, not merely filed.
propositions.quote: Justice Robert Barnes rejected that argument and concluded that second persons must address patents that have been found to be eligible for listing and added to the register, not patents that have merely been filed.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister relied on Eli Lilly 2009 FC 474, which held that only patents added to the register must be addressed by second persons.

propositions.text: The Regulations create a race between first and second persons to file patents and drug submissions.
propositions.quote: Serono describes the provisions of the Regulations as setting up a race between first persons and second persons.

propositions.text: Serono won the race by filing its patent lists before Apotex filed its drug submission.
propositions.quote: Serono says it won the race against Apotex. Serono filed its patent lists on March 16, 2023; Apotex filed its drug submission on March 22, 2023.

propositions.text: The one-week delay in adding Serono's patent to the register was due to the Minister's actions.
propositions.quote: Serono attributes the one-week delay in the addition of its patent to the register (on March 23, 2023) to the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: Serono claims the Regulations create a race, that it won by filing first, and blames the Minister for a one-week delay in listing its patent.

propositions.text: The Minister's one-week delay in adding the patent was unreasonable because the Regulations require immediate addition of eligible patents.
propositions.quote: Serono contends that the Minister’s decision to add the patent to the register a week after it was submitted was unreasonable because the Regulations do not admit of any discretion to delay – the Minister must simply add eligible patents to the register (s 3(2)).

propositions.text: Any delay risks depriving first persons of patent rights, contrary to the Regulations' intent.
propositions.quote: Serono argues that any delay between submission of an eligible patent and its listing on the register risks depriving first persons of their patent rights, contrary to the intent of the Regulations.

propositions.text: The Minister failed to consider Serono's argument about arbitrary delay and gave no explanation for the delay.
propositions.quote: Serono maintains that the Minister failed to consider its argument that the Minister had arbitrarily delayed adding the ‘419 patent to the register, to Serono’s prejudice, and that the Minister did not offer any explanation for the delay between March 16 and March 23.

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues the Minister unreasonably delayed listing its patent, risking its rights, and failed to address or explain the delay.

propositions.text: Serono proposes an alternative interpretation: second persons must address patents submitted before their drug submission, not just those added to the register.
propositions.quote: Serono contends that a second person must, therefore, address patents that were submitted by a first person before the second person filed its drug submission.

propositions.text: The critical date should be the patent's submission date, not the date it was added to the register.
propositions.quote: The critical date, according to Serono, is the date on which the first person submits a patent for addition to the register, not the date on which it was actually added.

propositions.text: Any other interpretation would fail to give meaning to the word 'submitted' in the Regulations.
propositions.quote: Serono argues that any other interpretation of the Regulations would be unreasonable because it would fail to give meaning to the word “submitted.”

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues second persons must address patents submitted before their drug submission, making the submission date the critical date under the Regulations.

propositions.text: Serono distinguishes its case from Eli Lilly, arguing it does not seek retroactive listing before eligibility, but immediate review and decision on eligibility.
propositions.quote: Serono says that its argument differs from Lilly’s: Serono does not contend that its patent should have been added to the register before it was found to be eligible – rather, it argues that the Minister had a duty to review and determine the patent’s eligibility immediately, not a week after it was submitted.

paragraphs.summary: Serono distinguishes its case from Eli Lilly, arguing it seeks immediate eligibility review, not retroactive listing before eligibility is determined.

propositions.text: Serono compares itself to Abbott, arguing its patent should be listed as of submission date or, alternatively, the date staff completed eligibility review.
propositions.quote: Serono argues that its patent should be added to the register as of the date on which it should have been added, namely, the date it was submitted. In the alternative, Serono proposes that its patent should have been added to the register on March 21, 2023, the date on which staff completed the screening and eligibility review form.

propositions.text: There is no justification for the two-day delay between staff review and the eligibility decision.
propositions.quote: There is no justification, says Serono, for the two-day delay between that review and the eligibility decision.

paragraphs.summary: Serono cites Abbott to argue for retroactive listing as of submission or staff review date, claiming no justification for the two-day delay.

propositions.text: Listing delays violate Canada's obligations under CUSMA, which requires a fair system for balancing first and second persons' interests.
propositions.quote: listing delays violate Canada’s obligations under the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement, 30 November 2018, Can TS 2020 No 5 (entered into force 1 July 2020) [CUSMA], which requires Canada to provide a fair system for balancing and litigating the interests of first and second persons.

propositions.text: The Minister's own SOP requires immediate examination of patents, if possible.
propositions.quote: the Minister’s own Standard Operating Procedure for Administration of the Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations states that the Minister must examine patents “immediately,” if possible.

paragraphs.summary: Serono claims listing delays breach CUSMA obligations and the Minister's SOP, both requiring prompt or immediate examination and balancing of interests.

propositions.text: IMC agrees the patent should have been added on March 21, 2023, when staff found it eligible.
propositions.quote: IMC concurs with Serono that the patent should have been added to the register on the date on which it was found by staff to be eligible – March 21, 2023.

propositions.text: The Minister's two-day delay in communicating the eligibility decision unreasonably penalized Serono.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s two-day delay in communicating the eligibility decision, in effect, unreasonably penalized Serono.

paragraphs.summary: IMC agrees with Serono that the patent should have been listed on March 21, 2023, and that the Minister's delay unfairly penalized Serono.

propositions.text: IMC submits second persons should address any patent submitted before their drug submission, reflecting the Regulations' purpose to protect eligible patents.
propositions.quote: IMC also submits that a second person should be required to address any patent that was submitted for addition to the register before the second person filed its drug submission. This requirement, says IMC, better reflects the purpose of the Regulations, which is to ensure that eligible patents are protected from infringement by second persons.

propositions.text: The Regulations recognize the public interest in drug innovation and patent value by granting first persons rights against second persons, including a 24-month stay.
propositions.quote: The Regulations recognize the strong public interest in encouraging drug innovation and the high commercial value of patents by granting first persons a right of action to protect their patent rights against second persons and a 24-month stay against second persons entering the market.

propositions.text: The Minister must interpret the Regulations reasonably and respect these significant interests.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, IMC maintains that the Minister must interpret the Regulations reasonably and with a view to respecting those significant interests.

paragraphs.summary: IMC argues second persons should address patents submitted before their drug submission, aligning with the Regulations' purpose and public interest in patent protection.

propositions.text: IMC argues requiring second persons to address patents submitted before their drug submission would not cause prejudice, as submissions can be updated.
propositions.quote: IMC argues that requiring a second person to address a patent submitted before, but added to the register after, the second person filed its drug submission would not cause any prejudice – second persons can always change or update their submissions to address those patents.

paragraphs.summary: IMC claims there is no prejudice in requiring second persons to address patents submitted before their drug submission, as submissions can be updated.

propositions.text: The Minister's decision was not unreasonable in the context of the Regulations, case law, and facts.
propositions.quote: The decision was not unreasonable in the context of the Regulations, the case law, and the facts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Minister's decision was not unreasonable given the Regulations, case law, and facts.

propositions.text: The Regulations' purposes and balance do not require immediate addition of patents or require second persons to address unlisted patents.
propositions.quote: I disagree that these factors point to an interpretation of the Regulations that would require the Minister to add patents to the register immediately upon submission, or after a preliminary review by staff, or that would require second persons to address patents that have not yet been added to the register.

propositions.text: The Minister has no discretion to delay adding patents, but does exercise discretion in determining eligibility for listing.
propositions.quote: The Minister does not have a discretion to delay adding patents to the register, but the Minister does exercise discretion in determining whether patents are eligible for listing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Regulations do not require immediate listing or addressing of unlisted patents, and the Minister's discretion is limited to eligibility decisions.

propositions.text: Interpreting the Regulations as Serono and IMC urge would require reading provisions in isolation, which is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: To interpret the Regulations in the manner urged by Serono and IMC, one would have to read certain provisions in isolation; that is not a reasonable approach to interpreting the Regulations.

propositions.text: Subsections 3(2) and 5(1), read in isolation, might suggest patents are added when submitted, but the Regulations say more.
propositions.quote: If the Regulations said no more, one might reasonably conclude that patents are added to the register when submitted, and that second persons must address those patents. But the Regulations do say more.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Serono and IMC's interpretation requires reading provisions in isolation, which is unreasonable, as the Regulations provide further context.

propositions.text: The register contains only patents the Minister has found eligible; patents are not added immediately upon submission.
propositions.quote: According to the Regulations, read as a whole, the patent register contains those patents the Minister has determined to be eligible for addition. Patents are not added to the register immediately upon submission.

propositions.text: Subsection 3(2) requires the Minister to add patents if eligible and refuse if ineligible.
propositions.quote: the Regulations require the Minister to “maintain a register of patents that have been submitted for addition to the register” by adding them to the register if they meet the eligibility requirements, and by refusing to add them if they are ineligible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds only eligible patents are added to the register, not immediately upon submission, as per subsection 3(2).

propositions.text: Second persons must address patents included on the register at the time of their submission, not those added later.
propositions.quote: Second persons need not address patents that get added to the register later (s 5(4)(a)).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds second persons only need to address patents on the register at their submission date, not those added later.

propositions.text: Serono and IMC's interpretation is unreasonable as it overlooks other provisions providing context for the Regulations.
propositions.quote: To read the Regulations in the limited way Serono and IMC urge me to do would be unreasonable because it would overlook the language in these other provisions that provide additional information and context for the provisions on which they rely.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Serono and IMC's interpretation unreasonable for ignoring contextual provisions in the Regulations.

propositions.text: The Minister reasonably relied on the 2006 RIAS, which supports requiring second persons to address only patents found eligible and added to the register.
propositions.quote: The Minister reasonably relied on the 2006 RIAS in support of this interpretation of the Regulations.

propositions.text: The 2006 RIAS states only patents meeting requirements are added to the register and second persons address only those on the register at filing date.
propositions.quote: Only those patents which meet the current timing, subject matter and relevance requirements set out in section 4 of the regulations are entitled to be added to Health Canada’s patent register and to the concurrent protection of the 24-month stay. […] [A] generic manufacturer that files a submission . . . is only required to address the patents on the register in respect of the innovative drug as of that filing date. Patents added to the register thereafter will not give rise to any such requirement. The register will thus be “frozen” in respect of that generic manufacturer’s regulatory submission. (2006 RIAS at pp 1511, 1519).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Minister reasonably relied on the 2006 RIAS, which supports addressing only eligible, listed patents at the time of submission.

propositions.text: The Minister reasonably relied on the Guidance Document, which clarifies patents are added only after eligibility review and second persons address only added patents.
propositions.quote: The Guidance Document, in the passages below, makes clear that patents are added to the register only after they have been reviewed and found to be eligible, and that second persons need only address patents that have actually been added

propositions.text: The Guidance Document states patents are added only after eligibility review and second persons address only those actually added.
propositions.quote: The requirements that must be met before a patent can be added to the Patent Register are provided by section 4 of the PM(NOC) Regulations (4.1, p 11). · The RMOD [Resource Management and Operations Directorate] will not add any patent... until it has completed a final evaluation and is satisfied that the patent... meets the eligibility requirements set out in section 4 (4.8, p 18). · The RMOD is required to add any patent on a patent list... that meets the requirements for addition to the Patent Register and to refuse to add any patent... that does not meet the requirements for addition to the Patent Register (7, p 28).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Minister reasonably relied on the Guidance Document, which confirms patents are added only after eligibility review and only those must be addressed.

propositions.text: The Minister's interpretation is supported by the Eli Lilly case, where backdating to submission was refused.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s interpretation is also supported by the Eli Lilly case, which he cited.

propositions.text: In Eli Lilly, the Minister refused to backdate the listing to the submission date, holding the proper date was when eligibility was found.
propositions.quote: The Minister refused that request, finding that the proper date for listing was the date on which the patent was found to be eligible – in November 2007.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Eli Lilly case supports the Minister's interpretation, as backdating to submission was refused in similar circumstances.

propositions.text: Justice Barnes found the Minister's decision in Eli Lilly correct, rejecting the argument for backdating to submission.
propositions.quote: Justice Barnes (there applying a standard of correctness, not unreasonableness) concluded that the Minister’s decision was correct.

propositions.text: Justice Barnes held that listing should occur contemporaneously with the Minister's eligibility determination, and second persons need not address patents added after their submission.
propositions.quote: The obvious intent of these provisions is that the listing of a patent on the register is to be done contemporaneously with the Minister’s determination of the patent’s eligibility for listing. The effect of this is that, under ss. 5(4), a second person need not address any patent added to the register after the date of the second person’s submission for a NOC under ss. 5(1) or ss. 5(2).

paragraphs.summary: Justice Barnes found the Minister's decision correct in Eli Lilly, holding listing occurs with eligibility determination and second persons need not address later-added patents.

propositions.text: Justice Barnes observed that delays between submission and listing burden first persons, but this was a legislative choice.
propositions.quote: Justice Barnes observed that the burden of any passage of time between submission and listing falls on first persons. But that was a legislative choice.

propositions.text: Justice Barnes found that requiring second persons to address ineligible patents would create problems.
propositions.quote: And the interpretation urged by Lilly would create its own problems by requiring second persons to address patents that are ineligible for listing.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Barnes noted delays burden first persons by legislative choice and that requiring second persons to address ineligible patents would cause problems.

propositions.text: Eli Lilly can be distinguished because it dealt with a patent first found ineligible, then eligible.
propositions.quote: Serono maintains that Eli Lilly can be distinguished from this case because it dealt with a situation where a patent was found first to be ineligible, and then eligible,

propositions.text: The difference identified by Serono is not relevant.
propositions.quote: I cannot see how that difference is relevant.

propositions.text: Justice Barnes interpreted the same provisions of the Regulations at issue here and I am bound by his interpretation unless there are strong reasons to believe he erred.
propositions.quote: Justice Barnes interpreted the same provisions of the Regulations that are in issue here and, subject to strong reasons to believe he erred, I am bound by his interpretation.

propositions.text: I see no error in Justice Barnes' judgment.
propositions.quote: I see no error in his judgment.

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues Eli Lilly is distinguishable, but the court finds the difference irrelevant, is bound by Justice Barnes' interpretation, and sees no error in his judgment.

propositions.text: The cases on which Serono relies are distinguishable.
propositions.quote: I find that the cases on which Serono relies are distinguishable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that the cases Serono relies on are distinguishable.

propositions.text: In Abbott, the Minister listed a patent, then delisted it after regulatory amendments, finding it ineligible.
propositions.quote: In the Abbott case, the Minister had originally listed Abbott’s patent in July 2006 but, after amendments to the Regulations in October 2006, the Minister found the patent no longer eligible for listing. He delisted it in February 2007.

propositions.text: Justice Simpson found the amendments gave the Minister power to delete ineligible patents, but found the patent was not ineligible.
propositions.quote: Justice Sandra Simpson found that the amendments specifically granted the Minister the power to delete from the register patents that were no longer eligible. However, she went on to find that the patent was not, in fact, ineligible for listing.

propositions.text: Justice Simpson ordered the patent be added as of the delisting date, not the original submission or listing date.
propositions.quote: She ordered that the patent be added to the register as of the date on which the Minister had delisted it. She did not, I note, order that the patent be added to the register as of the date it was originally submitted, or even as of the date it was originally listed.

propositions.text: Abbott does not assist in interpreting the Regulations at issue or advance Serono’s position.
propositions.quote: Abbott does not assist in interpreting the provisions of the Regulations in issue here; nor does it advance Serono’s position.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Abbott, noting it does not support Serono's position or assist in interpreting the relevant Regulations.

propositions.text: Serono cites Èquiterre v Canada (Health), 2016 FC 554.
propositions.quote: Serono also cites Èquiterre v Canada (Health), 2016 FC 554 [Èquiterre].

propositions.text: In Èquiterre, the Minister had a statutory obligation to begin a special review of pest control products banned by an OECD country.
propositions.quote: the Minister had a statutory obligation to begin a special review of any pest control products that were banned by an OECD country

propositions.text: Applicants asked the Minister to begin reviews; after months, the Minister refused for some products.
propositions.quote: The applicants asked the Minister to begin a number of special reviews of products prohibited in OECD countries; after several months, the Minister refused to initiate a review of some of them.

propositions.text: Justice Phelan held the Minister’s delay was unreasonable because the obligation arose immediately upon awareness of an OECD ban.
propositions.quote: Justice Michael Phelan held that the Minister’s delay was unreasonable because the obligation to initiate a special review arose immediately upon becoming aware of an OECD ban (para 58).

paragraphs.summary: Serono cites Èquiterre, where the court found the Minister's delay in starting a statutory review was unreasonable due to an immediate obligation.

propositions.text: Serono maintains the Minister must immediately review and add eligible patents to the register.
propositions.quote: Serono maintains that the same obligation arises here – the Minister must immediately review patents submitted by first persons and must add them to the register immediately upon determining them to be eligible.

propositions.text: Justice Phelan said the obligation arose immediately but required action within a reasonable time, not necessarily immediately.
propositions.quote: while Justice Phelan stated that the Minister’s obligation arose “immediately” upon becoming aware of an OECD ban, he went on to say that this obligation required the Minister to commence special reviews within a “reasonable time,” and declined to define what a “reasonable time” was (para 59).

propositions.text: Équiterre does not support Serono’s submission that the Minister must act immediately.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, Équiterre does not support Serono’s submission that the Minister must act “immediately.”

propositions.text: Health Canada screened Serono’s patent the day after submission; staff completed review form four days later.
propositions.quote: the evidence here shows that Health Canada screened Serono’s patent the day after it was submitted. Four days later, on March 21, 2023, staff completed the screening and eligibility review form.

propositions.text: The day staff completed the review form is not the Minister’s determination date.
propositions.quote: However, the day on which staff completed the screening and eligibility form is not the day of the Minister’s own determination of the patent’s eligibility to be listed.

propositions.text: The Minister added the patent to the register on the same day it was determined eligible, March 23, 2023.
propositions.quote: The Minister added the patent to the register on the same day that it was determined to be eligible, on March 23, 2023.

propositions.text: There was no delay.
propositions.quote: There was no delay.

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues for immediate action, but the court finds the law requires only reasonable time, notes prompt review, and finds no delay occurred.

propositions.text: The Minister’s interpretation of the Regulations was not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the Minister’s interpretation of the Regulations was not unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Regulations require the Minister to add eligible patents and refuse ineligible ones after determining if requirements are met.
propositions.quote: The Minister must add to the register those patents that meet the regulatory requirements, and must refuse to add patents that do not meet those requirements (ss 3(2)(a),(b)).

propositions.text: Once a patent is submitted, the Minister must determine if requirements are met; addition is not automatic and requires eligibility determination.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, once a patent has been submitted for addition to the register, the Minister must determine whether the regulatory requirements have been met (s 4(2)). The addition of a patent to the register is not automatic; it must await a determination of whether the patent is eligible.

propositions.text: Determining eligibility requires reviewing if the patent claims an approved medicinal ingredient, formulation, dosage form, or use.
propositions.quote: Determining eligibility requires a review of the patent to see whether it claims an approved medicinal ingredient, formulation, dosage form, or use.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Minister's interpretation reasonable and explains the Regulations require a determination of eligibility before adding a patent.

propositions.text: A second person must address patents submitted, reviewed, and added to the register by the Minister.
propositions.quote: A second person must address those patents that have been submitted by a first person, reviewed by the Minister and added to the register (ss 5(1),(2.1)).

propositions.text: A second person does not have to address a patent submitted but not yet added to the register.
propositions.quote: A second person does not have to address a patent that was submitted by a first person for addition to the register but not yet added to the register.

propositions.text: A second person need not address a patent added to the register on or after the date of their drug submission.
propositions.quote: Nor does a second person need to address a patent added to the register on or after the date of the second person’s drug submission (s 5(4)(a)).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains when a second person must address patents, depending on their status on the register.

propositions.text: The Minister’s decision to add Serono’s patent on the eligibility date was not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the Minister’s decision that Serono’s patent was properly added to the register on the date it was found to be eligible – March 23, 2023 – was not unreasonable.

propositions.text: When Apotex filed its submission on March 22, 2023, Serono’s patent was not yet on the register; Apotex had no obligation to address it.
propositions.quote: When Apotex filed its drug submission on March 22, 2023, Serono’s patent had not yet been added to the register; Apotex had no obligation to address it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Minister's timing reasonable and that Apotex had no obligation to address Serono's patent when it filed its submission.

propositions.text: The Minister’s decision to list Serono’s patent on the eligibility determination date was not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s decision to list Serono’s patent on the date on which the Minister determined it to be eligible for listing was not unreasonable given the facts and the regulatory context.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I must dismiss this application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Minister's decision reasonable and dismisses Serono's application for judicial review.

propositions.text: The parties agree costs should be determined by the middle of Column III of Tariff B, with no costs for or against interveners.
propositions.quote: The parties agree that costs should be determined in accordance with the middle of Column III of Tariff B in the Federal Courts Rules, SOR/98-106, with no costs to be awarded in favour of or against the interveners.

propositions.text: Parties may make submissions on costs within 10 days of the decision.
propositions.quote: Should the parties wish to make submissions to the Court on costs, they may do so within 10 days of the issuance of this decision.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed. Costs in favour of the respondents, to be determined by the middle of Column III of Tariff B.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is dismissed. Costs in favour of the respondents, shall be determined based on the middle of Column III of the Federal Court’s Tariff B.

propositions.text: Parties may make submissions on costs within 10 days of the judgment.
propositions.quote: The parties may make submissions on costs within 10 days of the issuance of this judgment.

paragraphs.summary: The court sets out the costs agreement, allows submissions on costs, and formally dismisses the application for judicial review with costs to respondents.
